:::{#thm-holder-inequality}
#### Holder's inequality

Let $(S, \salg, \measure)$ be a [measure space](#def-measure-space),
and let $p, q \in [1, \infty]$ be conjugate exponents satisfying $\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{q} = 1$
(with the convention that $q = \infty$ when $p = 1$, and $q = 1$ when $p = \infty$).
If $f \in L^p(\measure)$ and $g \in L^q(\measure)$ (@def-lp-space),
then their product $f g$ is [absolutely integrable](#def-absolutely-integrable) ($f g \in L^1(\measure)$) and satisfies:

$$
\norm{f g}_1 = \int_S \abs{f g} \, d\measure \le \norm{f}_p\,\norm{g}_q.
$$

When

$$
\begin{aligned}
p &= q \\
&= 2,
\end{aligned}
$$

this inequality is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for integrals.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-minkowski-inequality}
#### Minkowski's inequality ($L^p$ triangle inequality)

Let $(S, \salg, \measure)$ be a [measure space](#def-measure-space) and let $1 \le p \le \infty$.
For any functions $f, g \in L^p(\measure)$ (@def-lp-space), their sum $f + g$ is in $L^p(\measure)$ and satisfies:

$$
\norm{f + g}_p \le \norm{f}_p + \norm{g}_p.
$$

Together with absolute homogeneity $\norm{c f}_p = \abs{c}\,\norm{f}_p$ and definiteness,
Minkowski's inequality establishes that $L^p(\measure)$ satisfies all axioms of a [normed vector space](linear-algebra.qmd#def-norm).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-holder-inequality}
#### Applying Holder's inequality to finite sums and expectations

1. **Finite vectors (Cauchy-Schwarz and taxicab bounds)**:
   Equipping a finite set with the [counting measure](#def-counting-measure),
   Holder's inequality for conjugate exponents $p, q$ gives:
   $$
   \sumin \abs{x_i y_i} \le \paren{\sumin \abs{x_i}^p}^{1/p} \paren{\sumin \abs{y_i}^q}^{1/q}.
   $$
   Setting $p = 1$, $q = \infty$ gives $\sumin \abs{x_i y_i} \le \norm{\vx}_1\,\norm{\vy}_\infty$.
   Setting

   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   p &= q \\
   &= 2
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   gives the standard vector [Cauchy-Schwarz inequality](linear-algebra.qmd#thm-cauchy-schwarz).

2. **Covariance bound for random variables**:
   On a probability space with measure $\P$ (@def-probability-measure),
   taking

   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   p &= q \\
   &= 2
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   gives $\E{\abs{X Y}} \le \sqrt{\E{X^2}}\,\sqrt{\E{Y^2}}$,
   guaranteeing that the covariance between any two square-integrable random variables is finite.

:::
